claim: PI3Kγ is a critical immune signaling enzyme activated downstream of diverse cell surface molecules, including Ras, PKCβ activated by the IgE receptor, and Gβγ subunits released from activated GPCRs.
source: PI3Kγ is a critical immune signaling enzyme activated downstream of diverse cell surface molecules, including Ras, PKCβ activated by the IgE receptor, and Gβγ subunits released from activated GPCRs.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a background claim about PI3Kγ function.

claim: PI3Kγ can form two distinct complexes, with the p110γ catalytic subunit binding to either a p101 or p84 regulatory subunit.
source: PI3Kγ can form two distinct complexes, with the p110γ catalytic subunit binding to either a p101 or p84 regulatory subunit, with these complexes being differentially activated by upstream stimuli.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as established knowledge about PI3Kγ complex formation.

claim: The p110γ-p84 and p110γ-p101 complexes are differentially activated by upstream stimuli.
source: PI3Kγ can form two distinct complexes, with the p110γ catalytic subunit binding to either a p101 or p84 regulatory subunit, with these complexes being differentially activated by upstream stimuli.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as established knowledge.

claim: An allosteric inhibitory nanobody potently inhibits kinase activity through rigidifying the helical domain and regulatory motif of the kinase domain.
source: We defined the molecular basis for how an allosteric inhibitory nanobody potently inhibits kinase activity through rigidifying the helical domain and regulatory motif of the kinase domain.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract, supported by cryo-EM and biochemical data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The nanobody did not block either p110γ membrane recruitment or Ras/Gβγ binding.
source: The nanobody did not block either p110γ membrane recruitment or Ras/Gβγ binding, but instead decreased ATP turnover.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by TIRF microscopy data in Figure 1D-F.

claim: The nanobody decreased ATP turnover.
source: The nanobody did not block either p110γ membrane recruitment or Ras/Gβγ binding, but instead decreased ATP turnover.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by kinase activity assays.

claim: p110γ can be activated by dual PKCβ helical domain phosphorylation leading to partial unfolding of an N-terminal region of the helical domain.
source: We also identified that p110γ can be activated by dual PKCβ helical domain phosphorylation leading to partial unfolding of an N-terminal region of the helical domain.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract, supported by HDX-MS and mass spectrometry data in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: PKCβ phosphorylation is selective for p110γ-p84 compared to p110γ-p101.
source: PKCβ phosphorylation is selective for p110γ-p84 compared to p110γ-p101, driven by differential dynamics of the helical domain of these different complexes.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by mass spectrometry data in Figure 3E showing >100-fold lower phosphorylation of p110γ-p101.

claim: The selectivity of PKCβ phosphorylation for p110γ-p84 over p110γ-p101 is driven by differential dynamics of the helical domain of these different complexes.
source: PKCβ phosphorylation is selective for p110γ-p84 compared to p110γ-p101, driven by differential dynamics of the helical domain of these different complexes.
evidence: This is an interpretation stated in the abstract, supported by HDX-MS data showing different exchange kinetics in the helical domain.

claim: Nanobody binding prevented PKCβ-mediated phosphorylation.
source: Nanobody binding prevented PKCβ-mediated phosphorylation.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by mass spectrometry data in Figure 5A-B.

claim: The helical domain of p110γ has an allosteric regulatory role that is distinct between p110γ-p84 and p110γ-p101.
source: Overall, this work shows an unexpected allosteric regulatory role of the helical domain of p110γ that is distinct between p110γ-p84 and p110γ-p101 and reveals how this can be modulated by either phosphorylation or allosteric inhibitory binding partners.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion stated in the abstract, integrating multiple experimental findings.

claim: The helical domain of p110γ can be modulated by either phosphorylation or allosteric inhibitory binding partners.
source: Overall, this work shows an unexpected allosteric regulatory role of the helical domain of p110γ that is distinct between p110γ-p84 and p110γ-p101 and reveals how this can be modulated by either phosphorylation or allosteric inhibitory binding partners.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion stated in the abstract, integrating multiple experimental findings.

claim: Class I phosphoinositide 3 kinases (PI3Ks) are master regulators of myriad functions through their generation of the lipid signaling molecule phosphatidylinositol 3,4,5-trisphosphate (PIP3) downstream of cell surface receptors.
source: The class I phosphoinositide 3 kinases (PI3Ks) are master regulators of myriad functions through their generation of the lipid signaling molecule phosphatidylinositol 3,4,5-trisphosphate (PIP3) downstream of cell surface receptors (Burke and Williams, 2015; Rathinaswamy and Burke, 2020; Vanhaesebroeck et al., 2021; Vasan and Cantley, 2022).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Class I PI3Ks can be subdivided into the class IA and class IB subfamilies.
source: The class I PI3Ks can be further subdivided into the class IA and class IB subfamilies, with class IB PI3Ks being critical in immune signaling, and are composed of a single p110γ catalytic subunit that can bind to either a p101 or p84 regulatory subunit (Hawkins and Stephens, 2015; Lanahan et al., 2022; Okkenhaug, 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Class IB PI3Ks are critical in immune signaling.
source: The class I PI3Ks can be further subdivided into the class IA and class IB subfamilies, with class IB PI3Ks being critical in immune signaling, and are composed of a single p110γ catalytic subunit that can bind to either a p101 or p84 regulatory subunit (Hawkins and Stephens, 2015; Lanahan et al., 2022; Okkenhaug, 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Class IB PI3Ks are composed of a single p110γ catalytic subunit that can bind to either a p101 or p84 regulatory subunit.
source: The class I PI3Ks can be further subdivided into the class IA and class IB subfamilies, with class IB PI3Ks being critical in immune signaling, and are composed of a single p110γ catalytic subunit that can bind to either a p101 or p84 regulatory subunit (Hawkins and Stephens, 2015; Lanahan et al., 2022; Okkenhaug, 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The two PI3Kγ complexes (either p110γ-p84 or p110γ-p101) play essential and independent roles in both the adaptative and innate immune systems.
source: The two PI3Kγ complexes (either p110γ-p84 or p110γ-p101) play essential and independent roles in both the adaptative and innate immune systems.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge.

claim: Class IB PI3Kγ has shown promise as a therapeutic target, primarily as an immunomodulator of the tumor microenvironment leading to enhanced anti-tumor immune responses.
source: Class IB PI3Kγ has shown promise as a therapeutic target, primarily as an immunomodulator of the tumor microenvironment leading to enhanced anti-tumor immune responses (De Henau et al., 2016; Kaneda et al., 2016b).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Multiple isoform selective small molecule ATP competitive inhibitors of p110γ are in clinical trials for multiple forms of human cancers.
source: Multiple isoform selective small molecule ATP competitive inhibitors of p110γ are in clinical trials for multiple forms of human cancers (Li et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: All inhibitors currently developed toward p110γ act as ATP competitive inhibitors.
source: However, all inhibitors currently developed toward p110γ act as ATP competitive inhibitors, showing equal potency against both p110γ-p84 and p110γ-p101 complexes.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge.

claim: Current p110γ inhibitors show equal potency against both p110γ-p84 and p110γ-p101 complexes.
source: However, all inhibitors currently developed toward p110γ act as ATP competitive inhibitors, showing equal potency against both p110γ-p84 and p110γ-p101 complexes.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge.

claim: Knockout of both p101 and p84 leads to PIP3 levels that are equivalent to knockout of p110γ.
source: Detailed experiments on the role of p110γ in mice show that knockout of both p101 and p84 leads to PIP3 levels that are equivalent to knockout of p110γ, showing that all cellular PI3Kγ activities require the presence of either a p84 or p101 regulatory subunit (Rynkiewicz et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: All cellular PI3Kγ activities require the presence of either a p84 or p101 regulatory subunit.
source: Detailed experiments on the role of p110γ in mice show that knockout of both p101 and p84 leads to PIP3 levels that are equivalent to knockout of p110γ, showing that all cellular PI3Kγ activities require the presence of either a p84 or p101 regulatory subunit (Rynkiewicz et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: The two PI3Kγ complexes are differentially activated by membrane localized receptors, including G-protein coupled receptors, Ras, toll-like receptors, and the IgE antigen receptor.
source: The two complexes are differentially activated by membrane localized receptors, including G-protein coupled receptors (Li et al., 2000; Stephens et al., 1997), Ras (Jin et al., 2020; Kurig et al., 2009), toll-like receptors (Luo et al., 2018), and the IgE antigen receptor (Laffargue et al., 2002; Walser et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The different PI3Kγ complexes drive unique immune responses, with p110γ-p101 involved in chemotaxis in neutrophils, and p110γ-p84 involved in reactive oxide production.
source: This leads to the different complexes driving unique immune responses, with p110γ-p101 involved in chemotaxis in neutrophils (Bohnacker et al., 2009; Deladeriere et al., 2015), and p110γ-p84 involved in reactive oxide production.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Differential activation of unique PI3Kγ complexes downstream of GPCRs and Ras is caused by the ability of p101 to directly bind to Gβγ subunits downstream of activated GPCRs, with this being lost in p84.
source: Differential activation of unique PI3Kγ complexes downstream of GPCRs and Ras is caused by the ability of p101 to directly bind to Gβγ subunits downstream of activated GPCRs, with this being lost in p84, making p110γ-p84 activation by Gβγ dependent on Ras-mediated membrane recruitment (Rathinaswamy et al., 2023; Kurig et al., 2009; Rynkiewicz et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: p110γ-p84 activation by Gβγ is dependent on Ras-mediated membrane recruitment.
source: Differential activation of unique PI3Kγ complexes downstream of GPCRs and Ras is caused by the ability of p101 to directly bind to Gβγ subunits downstream of activated GPCRs, with this being lost in p84, making p110γ-p84 activation by Gβγ dependent on Ras-mediated membrane recruitment (Rathinaswamy et al., 2023; Kurig et al., 2009; Rynkiewicz et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Activation of PI3Kγ downstream of the IgE antigen receptor is driven by calcium-mediated activation of protein kinase C, leading to the selective phosphorylation and activation of p110γ at S582.
source: Activation of PI3Kγ downstream of the IgE antigen receptor is driven by calcium-mediated activation of protein kinase C, leading to the selective phosphorylation and activation of p110γ at S582 (Walser et al., 2013), with this putatively only occurring in p110γ-p84 and not in p110γ-p101.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: S582 phosphorylation putatively only occurs in p110γ-p84 and not in p110γ-p101.
source: Activation of PI3Kγ downstream of the IgE antigen receptor is driven by calcium-mediated activation of protein kinase C, leading to the selective phosphorylation and activation of p110γ at S582 (Walser et al., 2013), with this putatively only occurring in p110γ-p84 and not in p110γ-p101.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a hypothesis based on prior work.

claim: The full molecular mechanisms underlying how phosphorylation of p110γ is selective for different p84 or p101 complexes, and how it activates lipid kinase activity are poorly understood.
source: The full molecular mechanisms underlying how phosphorylation of p110γ is selective for different p84 or p101 complexes, and how it activates lipid kinase activity are poorly understood.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a knowledge gap.

claim: The p110γ catalytic subunit is composed of an adaptor binding domain (ABD), a Ras binding domain (RBD), a C2 domain, a helical domain, and a bi-lobal kinase domain.
source: The p110γ catalytic subunit is composed of an adaptor binding domain (ABD), a Ras binding domain (RBD), a C2 domain, a helical domain, and a bi-lobal kinase domain (Rathinaswamy et al., 2021a; Walker et al., 1999).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: A set of helices positioned C-terminal to the activation loop in the kinase domain play a critical role in regulating activity, referred to as the regulatory motif.
source: A set of helices positioned C-terminal to the activation loop in the kinase domain play a critical role in regulating activity, with this region referred to as the regulatory motif (Rathinaswamy et al., 2021c).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: The p110γ isoform is unique in that it is inhibited in the absence of a regulatory subunit.
source: The p110γ isoform is unique in that it is inhibited in the absence of a regulatory subunit, with this driven by an autoinhibitory conformation of the regulatory motif, that is proposed to require membrane association to disrupt (Gangadhara et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: The inhibition of p110γ in the absence of a regulatory subunit is driven by an autoinhibitory conformation of the regulatory motif, that is proposed to require membrane association to disrupt.
source: The p110γ isoform is unique in that it is inhibited in the absence of a regulatory subunit, with this driven by an autoinhibitory conformation of the regulatory motif, that is proposed to require membrane association to disrupt (Gangadhara et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: The regulatory motif is a common site of activating mutations in the other class I PI3K isoforms.
source: The regulatory motif is a common site of activating mutations in the other class I PI3K isoforms (Jenkins et al., 2023), with p110γ having rare activating oncogenic mutants in this region (Rathinaswamy et al., 2021c).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: p110γ has rare activating oncogenic mutants in the regulatory motif region.
source: The regulatory motif is a common site of activating mutations in the other class I PI3K isoforms (Jenkins et al., 2023), with p110γ having rare activating oncogenic mutants in this region (Rathinaswamy et al., 2021c).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: The p110γ subunit interacts with either p84 or p101 at an interface composed of the C2 domain, and the linkers between the RBD-C2 and C2-helical domains.
source: The p110γ subunit interacts with either p84 or p101 at an interface composed of the C2 domain, and the linkers between the RBD-C2 and C2-helical domains (Rathinaswamy et al., 2023).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: The p110γ-p84 complex forms a more dynamic complex compared to p110γ-p101.
source: The p110γ-p84 complex forms a more dynamic complex compared to p110γ-p101 (Rathinaswamy et al., 2023; Shymanets et al., 2013), however, no clear unique regulatory role of this difference in dynamics has been identified.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: No clear unique regulatory role of the difference in dynamics between p110γ-p84 and p110γ-p101 has been identified.
source: The p110γ-p84 complex forms a more dynamic complex compared to p110γ-p101 (Rathinaswamy et al., 2023; Shymanets et al., 2013), however, no clear unique regulatory role of this difference in dynamics has been identified.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a knowledge gap.

claim: The fundamental roles of p110γ in inflammatory processes have made it a therapeutic target in many pathological conditions, including asthma, arthritis, obesity, and cancer.
source: The fundamental roles of p110γ in inflammatory processes have made it a therapeutic target in many pathological conditions, including asthma (Campa et al., 2018), arthritis (Camps et al., 2005), obesity (Becattini et al., 2011; Breasson et al., 2017), and cancer (De Henau et al., 2016; Kaneda et al., 2016b; Kaneda et al., 2016a).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: There are significant side effects from non-isoform selective PI3Kγ inhibitors.
source: There are significant side effects from non-isoform selective PI3Kγ inhibitors (Bohnacker et al., 2017; Vanhaesebroeck et al., 2021), which has driven the development of highly p110γ selective small molecule inhibitors (Bell et al., 2012; Evans et al., 2016; Gangadhara et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: All p110γ inhibitors will target both p110γ-p101 and p110γ-p84.
source: However, all p110γ inhibitors will target both p110γ-p101 and p110γ-p84, so there is a potential for the development of allosteric inhibitors outside of the ATP binding site.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge.

claim: NB7 potently inhibited the membrane-mediated activation of p110γ-p84 by both Ras and Gβγ.
source: One from this group (denoted NB7 throughout the manuscript) potently inhibited the membrane-mediated activation of p110γ-p84 by both Ras and Gβγ, with HDX-MS experiments mapping the NB7 binding interface to the RBD, helical and kinase domains (Rathinaswamy et al., 2021b).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a supporting citation.

claim: HDX-MS experiments mapped the NB7 binding interface to the RBD, helical and kinase domains.
source: One from this group (denoted NB7 throughout the manuscript) potently inhibited the membrane-mediated activation of p110γ-p84 by both Ras and Gβγ, with HDX-MS experiments mapping the NB7 binding interface to the RBD, helical and kinase domains (Rathinaswamy et al., 2021b).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a supporting citation.

claim: All three forms of p110γ (p110γ, p110γ-p84, p110γ-p101) were potently inhibited by NB7.
source: Intriguingly, we found that all three forms of p110γ were potently inhibited by NB7 (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the Results section and supported by kinase assay data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The nanobody bound equivalently tightly to all complexes (p110γ, p110γ-p84, p110γ-p101), with ~2 nM potency.
source: The nanobody bound equivalently tightly to all complexes, with ~2 nM potency for p110γ, p110γ-p84, and p110γ-p101 (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the Results section and supported by BLI data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: There was no detectable binding of NB7 to p110α, p110β, and p110δ.
source: We also tested binding of the nanobody to all class IA PI3Ks, and there was no detectable binding to p110α, p110β, and p110δ (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the Results section and supported by BLI data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The nanobody had no effect on membrane recruitment of p110γ-p84 on bilayers containing membrane-tethered Ras (GTP) and Gβγ.
source: We found that the nanobody had no effect on membrane recruitment of p110γ-p84 on bilayers containing membrane-tethered Ras (GTP) and Gβγ (Figure 1D–F).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the Results section and supported by TIRF microscopy data shown in Figure 1D-F.

claim: A cryo-EM reconstruction of the complex of nanobody (NB7)-bound p110γ was obtained at 3.0 Å overall resolution from 149,603 particles.
source: Using this sample, we obtained a cryo-EM reconstruction of the complex of nanobody (NB7)-bound p110γ at 3.0 Å overall resolution from 149,603 particles (Figure 2A–D, Figure 2—figure supplements 1 and 2 and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the Results section and supported by cryo-EM data shown in Figure 2 and supplements.

claim: Nanobody binding did not induce any large-scale conformational changes of p110γ.
source: Nanobody binding did not induce any large-scale conformational changes of p110γ, as the structure of p110γ bound to NB7 was similar to the apo p110γ crystal structure or p110γ-p101 cryo-EM structure (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the Results section and supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: The interface between NB7 and p110γ was extensive, with ~1200 Å of buried surface area.
source: The interface between NB7 and p110γ was extensive, with ~1200 Å of buried surface area, with interactions of the ABD-RBD linker, N-terminus of the helical domain, and the regulatory motif at the turn between k8 and k9 (1022-1026aa).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the Results section based on structural analysis.

claim: The NB7 binding interface includes interactions with the ABD-RBD linker, N-terminus of the helical domain, and the regulatory motif at the turn between k8 and k9 (1022-1026aa).
source: The interface between NB7 and p110γ was extensive, with ~1200 Å of buried surface area, with interactions of the ABD-RBD linker, N-terminus of the helical domain, and the regulatory motif at the turn between k8 and k9 (1022-1026aa).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the Results section based on structural analysis.

claim: The location in the regulatory motif where NB7 binds is where both activating oncogenic (R1021C) and inhibitory loss of function mutants have been identified (R1021P).
source: This location in the regulatory motif is where both activating oncogenic (R1021C) and inhibitory loss of function mutants have been identified (R1021P) (Takeda et al., 2019), as well as a putative inhibitory phosphorylation site (T1024) (Perino et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with supporting citations.

claim: T1024 is a putative inhibitory phosphorylation site in the regulatory motif.
source: This location in the regulatory motif is where both activating oncogenic (R1021C) and inhibitory loss of function mutants have been identified (R1021P) (Takeda et al., 2019), as well as a putative inhibitory phosphorylation site (T1024) (Perino et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a supporting citation.

claim: The interface between NB7 and p110γ is primarily hydrophobic, with only 8 hydrogen bonds, and 1 electrostatic interaction among the 33 interfacial residues of NB7.
source: The interface is primarily hydrophobic, with only 8 hydrogen bonds, and 1 electrostatic interaction among the 33 interfacial residues of NB7.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the Results section based on structural analysis.

claim: Increased dynamics mediated by oncogenic mutants in the regulatory motif of p110γ increased kinase activity, putatively by breaking the autoinhibitory tryptophan lock in k12 of the regulatory motif.
source: Previous study of oncogenic mutants in the regulatory motif of p110γ showed that increased dynamics mediated by these mutants increased kinase activity, putatively by breaking the autoinhibitory tryptophan lock in k12 of the regulatory motif (Rathinaswamy et al., 2021c).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a supporting citation.

claim: Rigidifying the regulatory motif likely explains the molecular basis for how NB7 prevents kinase activity.
source: Therefore, rigidifying the regulatory motif likely explains the molecular basis for how it prevents kinase activity.
evidence: This is an interpretation stated in the Results section based on structural and prior functional data.

claim: The nanobody interface is distinct from the predicted Gβγ interface and the experimentally resolved Ras interface.
source: The nanobody interface is distinct from the predicted Gβγ interface (Rathinaswamy et al., 2023) and the experimentally resolved Ras interface (Pacold et al., 2000), explaining why it can still be membrane recruited by these stimuli.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with supporting citations and explains the TIRF microscopy observations.

claim: A phosphorylated peptide containing S582 was identified in PKCβ phosphorylation reactions on p110γ.
source: We identified a phosphorylated peptide containing S582, and surprisingly, we found an additional p110γ phosphorylation site at either S594/S595 (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the Results section and supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: An additional p110γ phosphorylation site at either S594/S595 was identified in PKCβ phosphorylation reactions.
source: We identified a phosphorylated peptide containing S582, and surprisingly, we found an additional p110γ phosphorylation site at either S594/S595 (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the Results section and supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Both p110γ and p110γ-p84 showed similar dose-response curves for PKCβ treatment, with similar curves for S582 and S594/S595.
source: Both p110γ and p110γ-p84 showed similar dose-response curves for PKCβ treatment, with similar curves for S582 and S594/S595.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the Results section and supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 3C-D.

claim: The p110γ-p101 complex was only very weakly phosphorylated, with <100-fold lower levels compared to p110γ and p110γ-p84.
source: The p110γ-p101 complex was only very weakly phosphorylated, with <100-fold lower levels compared to p110γ and p110γ-p84 (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the Results section and supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The weak phosphorylation of p110γ-p101 is consistent with the helical domain in p110γ being more rigid when bound to p101, compared to either bound to p84 or p110γ alone.
source: This is consistent with the helical domain in p110γ being more rigid when bound to p101, compared to either bound to p84 or p110γ alone.
evidence: This is an interpretation stated in the Results section based on the phosphorylation data and prior HDX-MS knowledge.

claim: The N-terminal region of the helical domain of apo p110γ (residues spanning 557-630aa) shows isotope profiles that are consistent with EX1 hydrogen-deuterium (H/D) exchange kinetics.
source: We have previously observed that the N-terminal region of the helical domain of apo p110γ (residues spanning 557-630aa) shows isotope profiles that are consistent with EX1 hydrogen-deutriuim (H/D) exchange kinetics (Rathinaswamy et al., 2021b; Rathinaswamy et al., 2021c; Vadas et al., 2013; Walser et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with supporting citations.

claim: EX1 H/D exchange kinetics is indicative of cooperative unfolding of extended protein regions, with H/D exchange occurring faster than the refolding event.
source: This is indicative of cooperative unfolding of extended protein regions, with H/D exchange occurring faster than the refolding event.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as established knowledge about HDX-MS.

claim: The EX1 kinetics in the helical domain may explain how the buried residues S582 and S594/S595 can be exposed to PKCβ.
source: This region is where the PKCβ phosphorylation sites are located and may explain how the buried residues S582 and S594/S595 can be exposed to PKCβ.
evidence: This is an interpretation stated in the Results section based on HDX-MS and phosphorylation data.

claim: p110γ-p101 does not show EX1 kinetics in the helical domain region, whereas both p110γ and p110γ-p84 do.
source: This is compatible with the observation that p110γ-p101 is protected from phosphorylation, as it does not show EX1 kinetics in this region, whereas both p110γ and p110γ-p84 do (Rathinaswamy et al., 2021a).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a supporting citation.

claim: Phosphorylated p110γ showed extensive increases in dynamics in the C2, helical domain, and kinase domain compared to unphosphorylated p110γ.
source: When we compared phosphorylated p110γ (>90.8% as measured by mass spectrometry at both sites) to unphosphorylated p110γ we observed extensive increases in dynamics in the C2, helical domain, and kinase domain (Figure 4A–D).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the Results section and supported by HDX-MS data shown in Figure 4A-D.

claim: The largest increases in exchange upon phosphorylation were located in the N-terminal region of the helical domain, with the peptides directly adjacent to the phosphorylation site showing almost complete deuterium incorporation at the earliest time points of exchange.
source: The largest increases in exchange upon phosphorylation were located in the N-terminal region of the helical domain, with the peptides directly adjacent to the phosphorylation site showing almost complete deuterium incorporation at the earliest time points of exchange.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the Results section based on HDX-MS data.

claim: The almost complete deuterium incorporation at the earliest time points in the N-terminal helical domain is indicative of significant disruption of the alpha helical secondary structure in this region.
source: This is indicative of significant disruption of the alpha helical secondary structure in this region.
evidence: This is an interpretation stated in the Results section based on HDX-MS data.

claim: Phosphorylated p110γ was enriched in the more fully deuterated species in the helical domain region.
source: When we examined the exchange profiles in this region, they still underwent EX1 kinetics (Figure 4C), however, phosphorylated p110γ was enriched in the more fully deuterated species.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the Results section and supported by HDX-MS data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: A portion of the regulatory motif of the kinase domain showed increased deuterium exposure upon phosphorylation.
source: In addition to the regions in the helical domain, a portion of the regulatory motif of the kinase domain also showed increased deuterium exposure.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the Results section based on HDX-MS data.

claim: The increases in exchange in the regulatory motif upon phosphorylation included the k9-k12 helices that surround the activation loop of p110γ.
source: This included the k9-k12 helices that surround the activation loop of p110γ.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the Results section based on HDX-MS data.

claim: The increases in exchange in the regulatory motif upon phosphorylation were similar to those observed in a R1021C oncogenic activating mutant of PIK3CG.
source: These increases in exchange were similar to those we had observed in a R1021C oncogenic activating mutant of PIK3CG (Rathinaswamy et al., 2021c).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a supporting citation.

claim: The p110γ enzyme in the absence of stimulators is very weakly active toward PIP2 substrate with only ~2-fold increased ATP turnover compared to in the absence of membranes.
source: The p110γ enzyme in the absence of stimulators is very weakly active toward PIP2 substrate with only ~2-fold increased ATP turnover compared to in the absence of membranes.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the Results section based on kinase activity assays.

claim: The weak activity of p110γ toward PIP2 substrate is consistent with very weak membrane recruitment of p110γ complexes in the absence of lipid activators.
source: This is consistent with very weak membrane recruitment of p110γ complexes in the absence of lipid activators (Rathinaswamy et al., 2023).
evidence: This is an interpretation stated in the Results section with a supporting citation.

claim: PKCβ-mediated phosphorylation enhanced the ATPase activity of p110γ ~2-fold in both the absence and presence of membranes.
source: PKCβ-mediated phosphorylation enhanced the ATPase activity of p110γ ~2-fold in both the absence and presence of membranes (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the Results section and supported by kinase activity assay data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The effect of phosphorylation is to change the intrinsic catalytic efficiency of phosphorylated p110γ, with limited effect on membrane binding.
source: This suggests that the effect of phosphorylation is to change the intrinsic catalytic efficiency of phosphorylated p110γ, with limited effect on membrane binding.
evidence: This is an interpretation stated in the Results section based on kinase activity assay data.

claim: The presence of NB7 showed a significant decrease in p110γ phosphorylation at both sites.
source: The presence of NB7 showed a significant decrease in p110γ phosphorylation at both sites (Figure 5A–B).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the Results section and supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 5A-B.

claim: There was no detectable binding of NB7 to phosphorylated p110γ.
source: BLI experiments showed that there was no detectable binding of NB7 to phosphorylated p110γ (Figure 5C–D), consistent with phosphorylation disrupting the N-terminal region of the p110γ helical domain.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the Results section and supported by BLI data shown in Figure 5C-D.

claim: The lack of NB7 binding to phosphorylated p110γ is consistent with phosphorylation disrupting the N-terminal region of the p110γ helical domain.
source: BLI experiments showed that there was no detectable binding of NB7 to phosphorylated p110γ (Figure 5C–D), consistent with phosphorylation disrupting the N-terminal region of the p110γ helical domain.
evidence: This is an interpretation stated in the Results section based on BLI and HDX-MS data.

claim: Lipid kinase assays using phosphorylated p110γ showed no detectable difference in activity when measured in the absence and presence of nanobody.
source: In addition, lipid kinase assays using phosphorylated p110γ showed no detectable difference in activity when measured in the absence and presence of nanobody (Figure 5E), consistent with NB7 being unable to bind to phosphorylated p110γ.

claim: The helical domain is a central regulator of the p110γ catalytic subunit of class IB PI3Kγ.
source: Here, we find that the helical domain is a central regulator of the p110γ catalytic subunit of class IB PI3Kγ, with modulation of helical dynamics through binding partners or PTMs able to either increase or decrease lipid kinase activity.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion stated in the Discussion section, integrating multiple experimental findings.

claim: Modulation of helical dynamics through binding partners or PTMs can either increase or decrease lipid kinase activity.
source: Here, we find that the helical domain is a central regulator of the p110γ catalytic subunit of class IB PI3Kγ, with modulation of helical dynamics through binding partners or PTMs able to either increase or decrease lipid kinase activity.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion stated in the Discussion section, integrating multiple experimental findings.

claim: The helical domain is a central regulator of class IA PI3Ks, where the nSH2 domain of the p85 regulatory subunits makes inhibitory interactions that significantly inhibit lipid kinase activity of all class IA catalytic subunits (p110α, p110β, and p110δ).
source: These results expand on previous work defining the helical domain as a central regulator of class IA PI3Ks, where the nSH2 domain of the p85 regulatory subunits makes inhibitory interactions that significantly inhibit lipid kinase activity of all class IA catalytic subunits (p110α, p110β, and p110δ) (Mandelker et al., 2009; Miled et al., 2007; Burke and Williams, 2013; Burke, 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with supporting citations.

claim: The inhibitory interaction between nSH2 and the helical domain in class IA PI3Ks is disrupted in human cancers (helical hotspot mutations in PIK3CA) and immune disorders (helical mutations in PIK3CD in APDS1).
source: This inhibitory interaction in class IA PI3Ks is disrupted in human cancers (helical hotspot mutations in PIK3CA) (Samuels et al., 2004) and immune disorders (helical mutations in PIK3CD in APDS1) (Angulo et al., 2013; Lucas et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with supporting citations.

claim: Class IB PI3Ks are unique compared to class IA PI3Ks, as they are not inhibited by p101 and p84 regulatory subunits, but instead potentiate GPCR activation.
source: Class IB PI3Ks are uniquely compared to class IA PI3Ks, as they are not inhibited by p101 and p84 regulatory subunits, but instead potentiate GPCR activation.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as established knowledge.

claim: The lack of inhibition of class IB PI3Ks by regulatory subunits is due to the distinct binding interface of class IB PI3K regulatory subunits compared to class IA regulatory subunits.
source: This lack of inhibition is due to the distinct binding interface of class IB PI3K regulatory subunits compared to class IA regulatory subunits, with only class IA regulatory subunits making direct inhibitory interactions with the kinase and helical domains of p110 catalytic subunits (Rathinaswamy et al., 2021a).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a supporting citation.

claim: A unique surface at the interface of the helical and kinase domains of p110γ is a potential site for the development of novel allosteric inhibitors that modulate p110γ activity.
source: Here, we show that a unique surface at the interface of the helical and kinase domains of p110γ is a potential site for the development of novel allosteric inhibitors that modulate p110γ activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Discussion section based on the structural and functional data.

claim: The nanobody interface is distinct from how the nSH2 inhibits class IA PI3K activity, as its binding site is on the opposite face of the helical domain.
source: The nanobody interface is distinct from how the nSH2 inhibits class IA PI3K activity, as its binding site is on the opposite face of the helical domain (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The mechanism of inhibition by NB7 is distinct from nSH2 inhibition, as the nSH2-helical interaction plays a critical role in preventing membrane recruitment of inhibited class I PI3Ks.
source: The mechanism of inhibition is also distinct, as the nSH2-helical interaction plays a critical role in preventing membrane recruitment of inhibited class I PI3Ks, with removal of this interface either through pYXXM motif binding or oncogenic mutations leading to increased membrane recruitment (Burke et al., 2012; Burke et al., 2011; Zhang et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with supporting citations.

claim: Nanobody binding does not sterically block complex formation with HRas or Gβγ.
source: Analysis of the nanobody binding site compared to the structure of HRas-p110γ or the HDX-MS supported Alphafold-multimer prediction of Gβγ-p110γ (Rathinaswamy et al., 2023) shows that nanobody binding does not sterically block complex formation (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The nanobody inhibited ATP turnover both in solution and on membranes, suggesting that it prevents formation of a catalytically competent conformation of p110γ, but still allows for membrane recruitment.
source: The nanobody inhibited ATP turnover both in solution and on membranes, suggesting that it prevents formation of a catalytically competent conformation of p110γ, but still allows for membrane recruitment.
evidence: This is an interpretation stated in the Discussion section based on kinase activity and TIRF microscopy data.

claim: Oncogenic mutations are frequent in the class IA PI3K encoded by PIK3CA, with this being the second most frequently mutated gene in human cancer.
source: Oncogenic mutations are frequent in the class IA PI3K encoded by PIK3CA, with this being the second most frequently mutated gene in human cancer (Lawrence et al., 2014).

claim: Mutations in p110γ encoded by PIK3CG in cancer are less frequent than in PIK3CA.
source: Mutations in p110γ encoded by PIK3CG in cancer are less frequent, however, they can still provide insight into regulatory mechanisms that control activity.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as established knowledge.

claim: Oncogenic mutations in the kinase domain (R1021C) and helical domain (E581K) are in close proximity to the nanobody binding site.
source: Oncogenic mutations in the kinase domain (R1021C) and helical domain (E581K) are in close proximity to the nanobody binding site, and both would be expected to disrupt the stability of the helical domain or regulatory motif of the kinase domain (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by structural mapping shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Oncogenic mutations R1021C and E581K would be expected to disrupt the stability of the helical domain or regulatory motif of the kinase domain.
source: Oncogenic mutations in the kinase domain (R1021C) and helical domain (E581K) are in close proximity to the nanobody binding site, and both would be expected to disrupt the stability of the helical domain or regulatory motif of the kinase domain (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is an interpretation stated in the Discussion section based on structural analysis.

claim: PKCβ is activated downstream of the IgE receptor in mast cells.

source: HDX-MS analysis of the helical domain of p110γ has shown that it is more dynamic than other class I PI3K isoforms (Burke and Williams, 2013; Walser et al., 2013), with the presence of the p101 regulatory subunit dramatically decreasing helical domain dynamics (Vadas et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with supporting citations.

claim: The presence of the p101 regulatory subunit dramatically decreases helical domain dynamics.
source: HDX-MS analysis of the helical domain of p110γ has shown that it is more dynamic than other class I PI3K isoforms (Burke and Williams, 2013; Walser et al., 2013), with the presence of the p101 regulatory subunit dramatically decreasing helical domain dynamics (Vadas et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a supporting citation.

source: This putative mechanism of helical domain dynamics driving PKCβ phosphorylation is consistent with our observation that p101 subunits decreased p110γ phosphorylation >100-fold.
